6.3 Curriculum Generation and Evaluation

The preceding experiments changed rewards, optimization settings, and demonstrations. We also compared two ways of choosing training tasks: increasing the frequency of existing tasks and using an LLM to generate new ones. The question is which tasks and behaviors benefit from the new curriculum.

Reweighted and Synthetic Curricula

Both runs start from the initial Qwen3-8B Instruct model. The reweighted curriculum uses the original 192 email training tasks. Eight samples per task determine its repetition count. For the 61 tasks with both successes and failures, each request template appears four times; for the other 131 tasks, each template appears once. Across four templates, this gives 61×4×4+131×4=1,50061\times4\times4+131\times4=1,50061×4×4+131×4=1,500 training inputs. Task rules and scoring remain those of the original environment.

For the synthetic curriculum, DeepSeek-v4-flash proposes email-task variants from execution branches and specifies required actions, forbidden actions, and terminal outcomes. The variants use parameters of the existing environment, such as additional candidate contacts, changed sharing rules, or retrieval faults. The model then generates a solution, which code checks against the accompanying rules. The final dataset contains 10 synthetic task entries whose solutions pass the checks, each repeated 92 times, plus 580 records sampled from the original training inputs: 1,500 rows in total.

Each synthetic training prompt contains only the system message and task request. Task-construction parameters, scoring rules, and generated solutions are stored as training metadata. GRPO samples fresh actions for these tasks; the completed curriculum uses the accompanying rules to score them.

Both curricula receive five epochs of GRPO, totaling 230 steps, with 32 inputs per batch and eight rollouts per input at temperature 1.0. Appendix C.1.5 gives the remaining settings. This comparison changes both training content and the scoring rules for synthetic tasks; its objects are the two curriculum recipes.

Fixed Scoring Rules for Synthetic Tasks

The initial synthesis procedure asked an LLM to judge whether each solution was correct. We resubmitted 46 previously accepted trajectories to the same DeepSeek-v4-flash model. Two repeat judgments accepted only 13/46 and 12/46. DeepSeek-v4-pro accepted 35/46. Each fraction counts how many previously accepted trajectories were accepted again.

The completed synthetic-curriculum run instead executes scoring rules supplied when each task is generated. For example, one synthetic task with sharing forbidden requires contact and file retrieval, clarification of file identity, and termination. Sending, drafting, and requesting confirmation are forbidden. Scoring checks these requirements and whether the terminal outcome is a send, a draft, or no write.

The synthetic reward is a weighted mean of binary checks. Branch order, terminal outcome type, and absence of blocked actions each receive weight 2; the remaining checks receive weight 1. The order check compares only non-clarification actions. Clarification is scored separately by occurrence, and terminal comparison distinguishes only send, draft, or no write. A generated solution is retained only if all checks pass; training uses the weighted score directly. Fixed rules make repeated scoring of the same trajectory deterministic; whether those rules fully express the task depends on their content. The early repeat-judgment experiment and the completed curriculum therefore use different scoring procedures.

Evaluation on Original and Synthetic Tasks

We evaluate both curricula on 68 fixed tasks from the original email suite and 13 separately generated task records. The former use the original deterministic evaluator; the latter use their accompanying scoring rules. These 13 records derive from five seed tasks, four of which also generated the 10 synthetic training records. Comparing the combined seed, variant index, construction parameters, and scoring rules finds no exact record overlap between training and evaluation, although they share seed tasks.

Six of the 10 synthetic task entries are derived from two tasks among these 68. We therefore use the 68 tasks as a fixed reference set whose task sources partly overlap with those of the synthetic curriculum.

Evaluation set Reweighted curriculum Synthetic curriculum
68 fixed tasks from the original suite 64/68 63/68
13 separately generated task records 0/13 6/13

The synthetic curriculum passes more generated tasks and completes one fewer original fixed task. Both task content and scoring differ between the sets. The results show that the observed curriculum benefit depends on what is evaluated.

Action Order on New Tasks

The synthetic curriculum completes 40/60 information-relocation tasks, compared with 15/60 for the reweighted curriculum. Adding a source pointer gives 34/60 versus 10/60. Success counts are also higher on the two numerical task sets, but fewer trajectories match the interaction signature.

Added source pointer 10/60 34/60 10/60 40/60
Two-tool numerical comparison 28/60 30/60 38/60 3/60
Both numbers returned by the policy tool 19/60 22/60 27/60 6/60

Part II. Intermediate Signals and Group-Relative Credit

Chapter 7. Visit Rewards and Content Responses in WebShop

7.1 WebShop Tasks, Rewards, and Text Treatments

In our WebShop experiments, we add a reward for visiting product subpages, aiming to encourage the model to obtain information before buying and use it to choose products that better match the user's requirements.

Page-visit frequency measures whether the model learns the retrieval action. The content-treatment experiment changes page text and compares purchase fields and action sequences. We first define the fields, then interpret the results accordingly. We also decompose attribute scores for purchased products to locate matched attributes across pages.

Task and terminal score

This section compares three GRPO models trained from the initial Qwen3-8B Instruct model to step 75. The first uses only terminal reward. The second adds a 0.08 page-visit reward. The third grants that visit reward only when the final purchase receives full task reward. These are separate training runs used to compare how the reward condition affects retrieval behavior.

WebShop simulates a shopping website. After receiving the user's purchase requirements, the model starts from the search page and operates the website through text commands. The system executes each command and returns the page content to the model.

Command Effect
search[query] Search for products using a model-generated query
click[B0XXXXXXXX] Open the corresponding product's detail page
click[option value] Select a variant such as color or size
click[description], click[features], click[reviews], click[attributes] Open a product subpage for additional information
click[back to search], click[< prev], click[next >] Go back or change page
click[buy now] Purchase the current product and end the task

The model generates the query in search[...] and selects the target of click[...] from the clickable items shown on the page. In this experiment, each task allows at most 15 actions and ends after a purchase or when the action budget is exhausted.

WebShop computes the terminal score from the purchased product and selected options.

Terminal score=Matched attributes+Correct options+Price scoreRequired attributes+Required options+1×Type-match coefficient. \text{Terminal score} = \frac{ \text{Matched attributes}+\text{Correct options}+\text{Price score} }{ \text{Required attributes}+\text{Required options}+1 } \times\text{Type-match coefficient}. Terminal score=Required attributes+Required options+1Matched attributes+Correct options+Price score​×Type-match coefficient.

The price score is 1 when the price does not exceed the user's limit and 0 otherwise. The type-match coefficient takes values 0,0.1,0.5,10, 0.1, 0.5, 10,0.1,0.5,1 according to title, category, and query matching. The exact rules appear under “WebShop Type-Match Coefficient” in Appendix B.1.

For example, the user requires two product attributes, one option, and a price limit, giving four requirements. If the purchased product matches one attribute, the option and price are correct, and its type fully matches, the score is 3/43/43/4.

Visit reward

We reward visits to four product subpages: description, features, reviews, and attributes. Opening any one of these subpages before buying the product satisfies the visit condition. Repeated visits or visits to multiple subpages count only once.

The visit and purchase must concern the same product. For example, reading product A's description and then buying product B does not earn the reward. The model must visit B's subpage before buying B. Without a completed purchase, there is no visit reward.

Let ppp denote the visit-condition measure, calculated from purchases satisfying the condition above.

p=Purchases satisfying the visit conditionPurchases. p=\frac{\text{Purchases satisfying the visit condition}}{\text{Purchases}}. p=PurchasesPurchases satisfying the visit condition​.

If no purchase occurs, p=0p=0p=0. WebShop usually ends after the first valid purchase, so ppp normally takes one of two values: 1 if the model visited that product's subpage before buying it, and 0 otherwise. Page openings are counted separately to check for repeated visits.

We compare two reward schemes. The first gives a bonus whenever the visit condition is met. Let GGG denote the terminal score and λ\lambdaλ the visit-reward coefficient. The training reward is

R=G+λp. R=G+\lambda p. R=G+λp.

The second adds a score threshold ggg and gives the visit bonus only when the terminal score reaches that threshold.

R={G+λp,G≥g,G,G<g. R= \begin{cases} G+\lambda p, & G\ge g,\\ G, & G<g. \end{cases} R={G+λp,G,​G≥g,G<g.​

When g=1g=1g=1, the model must make a full-score purchase to receive the visit bonus.

The default visit bonus is 0.080.080.08. For tasks with scoring denominator at most 12, a non-full-score purchase plus the bonus remains below a full-score purchase without a visit: 11/12+0.08≈0.997<111/12+0.08\approx0.997<111/12+0.08≈0.997<1. Rankings between partial scores can still change, for example 0.025+0.08>0.1000.025+0.08>0.1000.025+0.08>0.100.

The following are actual trajectories from two models completing the same purchase task. One reads the product description and features before buying; the other buys directly.

Visit subpages before buying:

search[noise cancelling cosycost usb microphone under 70]
→ click[B0972Q1T8T]
→ click[description]
→ click[< prev]
→ click[features]
→ click[< prev]
→ click[buy now]

Buy directly:

search[noise cancelling cosycost usb microphone under 70]
→ click[B0972Q1T8T]
→ click[buy now]

Both trajectories buy the same product and receive a terminal score of 1. With the visit bonus, the first receives 1.081.081.08 and the second still receives 111. Opening two subpages earns the first trajectory only one bonus of 0.080.080.08.

Evaluation methods

Task evaluation runs each model once per task and saves terminal scores and page-visit information. Trajectory replay re-executes saved actions to check whether visits return nonempty content. The content-treatment experiment runs separate text conditions for the same task and saves action sequences and purchase fields. Product-score decomposition examines the products actually purchased to locate matched attributes in titles and subpages.

Content-treatment experiment

The script starts a separate run from the initial page for each task and condition. It does not save an intermediate state and branch into two continuations. Every qualifying observation is processed, so a trajectory may receive treated content more than once.

Condition Treatment
Reference, null Replace Rating: N.A. with Rating: 4.3; otherwise replace the first Rating: with Rating: 4.3 —, retaining the original rating that follows
price Set the detail-page price to three times the user's budget
note Append a product-mismatch statement to detail pages
desc Append information conflicting with the request to subpages
note_sub Append a product-mismatch statement to subpages

The script selects null as a reference because it treats star ratings as outside the task requirements; this condition still changes model-visible text. A comparison with a subpage condition can therefore differ at an earlier detail page. For each pair, we compare action sequences, target products, and treatment counts to check whether the runs already differed before the treatment.

The desc condition fills the templates This product is NOT {attributes}. and It is not available in {options}. with the task's attributes and options. If both are absent, it falls back to an over-budget or generic mismatch statement. In contrast, note and note_sub always append NOTE: This item does NOT match your request.; only their placement differs. Subpage treatment is triggered when the preceding click is description, features, or reviews, excluding attributes.

The script assigns each run's target from its first call of the form click[b0…]. Subsequent page treatments do not check again that the current product is this target. The saved bought_target field is true when the environment reports termination and the last such product click in the action sequence points to that run's target. This Boolean indicates only whether this condition holds; the full identity of the final purchased product is absent from this Boolean field.

We pair runs by task ID, retaining tasks with evaluation outputs under both conditions and fired=true in both runs. This field means that page text changed at least once. We calculate

Purchase-field change rate=Pairs with different bought_target valuesPairs with text treatment triggered in both runs. \text{Purchase-field change rate} =\frac{\text{Pairs with different bought\_target values}} {\text{Pairs with text treatment triggered in both runs}}. Purchase-field change rate=Pairs with text treatment triggered in both runsPairs with different bought_target values​.

Eligibility depends on whether each run reaches a treated page. Section 7.2 separately compares purchase Booleans, target products, and action sequences across the paired runs.

Attribute-score decomposition of purchased products

For the product actually purchased in each replayable trajectory, we check whether requested attributes occur in its title, Description, or BulletPoints. The att_subpage_only field counts requested attributes absent from the title but present in Description or BulletPoints. These are attributes already matched by this purchased product.

For each purchase trajectory included in the decomposition, we compute

Subpage-matched attribute share=Requested attributes matched in Description or BulletPoints but not the titleRequired attributes+Required options+1. \text{Subpage-matched attribute share} =\frac{\text{Requested attributes matched in Description or BulletPoints but not the title}} {\text{Required attributes}+\text{Required options}+1}. Subpage-matched attribute share=Required attributes+Required options+1Requested attributes matched in Description or BulletPoints but not the title​.

For example, two attributes, one option, and a price limit give four scoring components. If one requested attribute of the purchased product matches only in those subpage texts, the share is 1/41/41/4. The calculation omits the product-type coefficient and describes a share of scoring components.

We retain tasks with a score decomposition whose replayed score matches the saved terminal score, then calculate the mean, median, and zero count. This quantity describes the attribute-score composition of the products actually purchased and varies with those products and the replayable task set. Benefits from switching products, rejecting unsuitable products, or changing options after reading are forms of information value outside this decomposition.

Page visits and returned content

We compare three training schemes: terminal reward alone, an added visit reward, and a visit reward given only for full-score purchases. Each model runs once on the same 500 tasks, yielding 500, 499, and 498 trajectories, respectively, that can be parsed and produce an environment outcome. The table uses each model's valid task count as its denominator.

Adding the visit reward raises page visitation from 18.8% to 99.8% and task success from 42.8% to 44.3%. Restricting the bonus to full-score purchases still produces 99.4% visitation, with task success at 41.2%. Both reward schemes make the model visit a subpage before almost every purchase, while task success changes much less.

We examine whether the model continues comparing other products after visiting a subpage, to understand the role of retrieval in the purchase process. The model trained with the full-score gate commonly follows this action sequence.

open product details
→ view rewarded subpage
→ return to product detail
→ buy the same product

Subpage visits occur mainly in the final steps before purchase, with little further browsing of other products afterward.

For the first six models, the visitation proportion ranges from 5.3% to 26.1%. Qwen3.7-plus exhausts the 15-step budget on 158/200 tasks, and only 48 trajectories complete a purchase. Its 4/48 describes the minority of tasks reaching purchase and needs to be read alongside its low completion count.

Without this project's visit-reward training, these models also often buy directly. Low page visitation is therefore not confined to our terminal-reward model.

Evidence on Visitation and Content Use

The visit reward makes pre-purchase subpage visits nearly universal, and replay confirms that they usually return nonempty content. Task success changes much less than visitation, while the full-score-gated model usually visits near the end of its purchase procedure.

The text-treatment experiment compares purchase-field responses across conditions. It does not establish the stronger claim that the model learned retrieval without learning to use information. The attribute decomposition describes matches in purchased products, leaving the benefit of reading before product selection unmeasured.

Chapter 8. Reward Signals in Group-Relative Training

8.1 Group Advantages and Behavioral Differences

When errors remain, do the trajectories sampled for a task provide GRPO with a signal for improvement? We group saved trajectories by task, compare returns and actions, and calculate advantages. Different procedures receiving the same score and repetition of one procedure call for different next checks.

Advantage calculation

For this audit, we sample eight T=1.0T=1.0T=1.0 rollouts per prompt and recompute standard GRPO advantages from the saved rewards. Each trajectory's advantage is

A=R−Rˉs+10−6. A=\frac{R-\bar R}{s+10^{-6}}. A=s+10−6R−Rˉ​.

Here, RRR is this trajectory's reward, while Rˉ\bar RRˉ and sss are the mean and sample standard deviation of the eight rewards in the group. The 10−610^{-6}10−6 term prevents division by zero. Rewards above the group mean yield positive advantages; rewards below it yield negative advantages.

Standard GRPO applies the trajectory's advantage to each generated token that participates in training. Model-generated content enters the loss calculation; observations returned by tools do not.

First consider the ordinary clipped policy term for each token participating in training:

ℓ=−min⁡(ρA, clip⁡(ρ,1−ϵlo,1+ϵhi)A). \ell=-\min\left(\rho A,\ \operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{hi}})A\right). ℓ=−min(ρA, clip(ρ,1−ϵlo​,1+ϵhi​)A).

AAA is the advantage of the trajectory containing this token. ρ\rhoρ is the ratio of the current-policy probability to the old-policy probability for this token in the same context. Here, the old-policy probability is recomputed by the actor; probabilities recorded by the rollout engine are used separately for discrepancy diagnostics. The two ϵ\epsilonϵ values control the lower and upper clipping bounds for this ratio.

The runs also apply dual clipping to the negative-advantage branch; Appendix B gives the complete formula. The resulting token losses are averaged over all tokens participating in training to obtain the reward-derived policy loss.

When a trajectory's advantage is zero, it no longer supplies an update signal through the policy loss above. KL regularization may still drive model updates, so the reward-derived policy loss and the KL term need to be checked separately. Implementation details are in Appendix B.

Within-group reward differences

To inspect the training signal, we need to examine rewards separately for each prompt. For example, a training batch could contain these three groups of trajectories.

Prompt A: 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2
Prompt B: 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10
Prompt C: 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18, 18

Rewards across the batch range from 2 to 18, but all eight trajectories for each prompt have the same score. GRPO computes advantages separately within each group, so all advantages in these three groups are zero.

We evaluate a WebShop model after GRPO training with terminal reward only. We sample eight T=1.0T=1.0T=1.0 rollouts for each of 500 tasks. On 403 tasks, all eight trajectories receive exactly the same score.

Scores of the eight trajectories Tasks
All receive the full score of 1 192
All receive 0 14
Identical scores strictly between 0 and 1 197
Total tasks with tied scores 403/500

On 197 of these tasks, the scores remain below full credit, leaving room for improvement. However, all eight trajectories for each task have the same score, so every group advantage is zero. Under the current reward, these samples provide GRPO with no signal for improvement.

Action differences

Tied scores can come from different procedures or from the model repeating identical actions. We compare the eight trajectories for each of the 500 tasks above, counting their actions as identical only when the action names, arguments, and order all match.

Scores across eight trajectories Actions across eight trajectories Tasks
All identical All identical 235
All identical Some differ 168
Some differ Some differ 97
Some differ All identical 0

Of the 403 tasks with tied scores, 235 have exactly the same actions in all eight runs. This also holds for 121 of the 197 tied tasks below full score. The model has room to improve on these tasks but repeats the same procedure across all eight samples.

Repeated Actions and Different Choices in Tied Tasks

Substituting a tied group's returns into the formula gives zero advantage for all eight trajectories. The next two examples have returns of 0.5 and 0.1 respectively, but differ in their action variation.

For the first task, all eight runs follow this action chain and score 0.5.

search[long clip-in hair extension natural looking]
→ click[b08h5dcd65]
→ click[natural black #1b]
→ click[buy now]

In all eight trajectories, the model chooses the same product and option. Applying the same deterministic scoring rule to the same task and action chain still gives identical scores. To compare another purchase procedure, first inspect why sampling repeats and whether the available candidates offer different actions. This comparison concerns environment actions, not all generated model tokens.

For the second task, all eight trajectories score 0.1 and share the opening calls.

search[gluten free popcorn]
→ click[b08frlyzfd]
→ click[description]
→ click[back to search]
→ search[gluten free popcorn under 140]
→ click[b08vy7qx9s]

1 rollout:  click[sea-salt]        → click[buy now]
7 rollouts: click[sweet-and-salty] → click[buy now]

Two flavor choices are already present. The next check is the user request and its scoring components: does this difference deserve a reward difference? The sampling file preserves actions and returns, but not the complete request, so this example does not prescribe which flavor should score higher. Favoring an arbitrary flavor just to break the tie would mistake behavioral variation for task progress.

These tasks present different training problems. Where relevant action differences exist, reward determines how to distinguish them. Where saved actions are identical, another procedure to compare is missing. Task requirements determine which action differences merit reward.

How reward changes affect advantages

If every trajectory in a group receives the same additional reward ccc, the mean reward also increases by ccc, while the standard deviation stays unchanged. Subtracting the mean removes this constant when computing the advantage.

A′=(R+c)−(Rˉ+c)s+10−6=A. A'=\frac{(R+c)-(\bar R+c)}{s+10^{-6}}=A. A′=s+10−6(R+c)−(Rˉ+c)​=A.

Adding or subtracting the same amount from every trajectory's reward therefore leaves the group's advantages unchanged.

For example, adding 0.08 for a visit and subtracting 0.08 for no visit differ only by a uniform deduction.

Visited? Visit bonus No-visit penalty
Yes Original reward + 0.08 Original reward
No Original reward Original reward − 0.08

The right column is always 0.08 below the left. This difference disappears when computing group advantages, so the two reward schemes produce identical advantages for the same trajectories.

Increasing the reward coefficient does not necessarily increase the advantage. Suppose all trajectories in a group have the same terminal score ccc and differ only in their process score qqq. Their total reward is

R=c+λq,λ>0. R=c+\lambda q, \qquad \lambda>0. R=c+λq,λ>0.

Increasing λ\lambdaλ scales both the reward differences and their standard deviation. Substituting into the advantage formula gives

A=q−qˉsq+10−6/λ, A=\frac{q-\bar q}{s_q+10^{-6}/\lambda}, A=sq​+10−6/λq−qˉ​​,

where qˉ\bar qqˉ​ and sqs_qsq​ are the mean and sample standard deviation of the process scores in the group. When the numerical stabilizer has a negligible effect, increasing the positive coefficient barely changes the advantage.

If all eight trajectories visit the page and receive the same visit bonus, that bonus becomes a constant within the group. Increasing it further does not change the advantages. If the terminal scores are also identical, all eight advantages are zero.

When both terminal and process scores vary within the group, adjusting the coefficient changes their relative influence on the total reward. The full derivation is in Appendix B.

Breaking the total reward into component scores shows what each of two tied trajectories gets right. For example, one selects the correct color but exceeds the budget; the other stays within budget but selects the wrong color. If color and price are each worth one point, the trajectories receive the same total score.

Making training favor one of these choices requires changing the scoring rule. Increasing the weight on color, for example, gives the first trajectory a higher score. The new ordering comes from prioritizing color.

Zero-Advantage Training Steps in Ask-or-Act

The preceding results come from post-training sampling. To inspect zero advantages during training, we analyze the Ask-or-Act prompt-group state-baseline run group-phi-k0, using askact_group_phi and c1-train.parquet. The log later contains a separate WebShop run. We first select the Ask-or-Act segment by launch markers, then retain the first record for each training step, obtaining 230 steps.

In 136 of the 230 steps, all advantages and the corresponding policy loss are zero. This occurs for 35 consecutive steps from 130 through 164. Training continues, but these steps receive no policy update signal from the sampled rewards.

Across these 136 steps, the KL loss remains nonzero, with a mean of 0.0827 and a range of 0.0627–0.1026. KL regularization may continue driving model updates, but task reward no longer guides these steps through group advantages. Checking whether training is still learning the target behavior therefore requires inspecting advantages and policy loss separately.

The following experiments try to improve sampling and scoring, testing whether these changes can provide an effective training signal for the target behavior.

8.2 Scoring and Training Intermediate Actions

To help the model learn correct intermediate actions, we try changing how actions are scored and how those scores are used in training. The experiments examine both whether the training signal changes and whether the model performs better on held-out tasks.

These attempts intervene at different points. The table identifies their inputs and direct changes before the formulas and behavioral results.

Attempt Inputs Direct change
GiGPO Actions and subsequent returns at the same state within a prompt Add local advantages to episode advantages
Group-external action value States, action categories, and terminal returns from historical training trajectories Add table-based action advantages to current tied groups
Correct-answer scoring Required options for the current task and generated option actions Add option-correctness scores to the corresponding action advantages
State baseline Pre-action environment fact ledger and preceding actions Subtract a state baseline from terminal return
Shuffled state baseline The same collection of baseline values Change the state-to-value mapping and train again
Token-length analysis Loss-aggregation formula and logged length statistics Calculate weights after the fact; no new aggregation-rule training run

The first five are training comparisons; the last is calculation and log analysis. None directly constructs new candidate actions for the current prompt. Once scores are nonzero, we still need to inspect what the model generated and how advantages apply to those actions.

GiGPO action advantages

Standard GRPO uses the same advantage for all generated tokens in a trajectory. GiGPO additionally compares actions taken from the same state and computes local advantages from the rewards obtained afterward.

For example, several trajectories for the same task reach the same product page. Some continue reading information, while others buy directly. GiGPO compares these actions and applies each local advantage only to the generated tokens of the corresponding action.

Starting from the current action, we discount subsequent rewards by their distance and sum them to obtain the action's discounted return.

Q=r0+γr1+γ2r2+⋯+γnrn. Q=r_0+\gamma r_1+\gamma^2r_2+\cdots+\gamma^n r_n. Q=r0​+γr1​+γ2r2​+⋯+γnrn​.

Here, r0r_0r0​ is the current action's reward, r1r_1r1​ is the next action's reward, and rnr_nrn​ is the final action's reward. We use γ=0.95\gamma=0.95γ=0.95: each additional step before a reward is received multiplies its contribution to the current action by another 0.950.950.95.

The implementation determines whether states match using the current page content and the preceding purchase and subpage-visit counts. Actions are compared only when they share the same prompt, page content, and counts.

In this experiment, we add the trajectory and local advantages directly, without dividing by the standard deviation.

A=(G−Gˉ)+(Q−Qˉ). A=(G-\bar G)+(Q-\bar Q). A=(G−Gˉ)+(Q−Qˉ​).

GGG is the return of the complete trajectory, and Gˉ\bar GGˉ is the mean trajectory return for the same prompt. QQQ is the current action's discounted return, and Qˉ\bar QQˉ​ is the mean discounted return of actions taken under the same prompt and state.

The first term compares complete trajectory outcomes; the second compares subsequent outcomes from the same state.

If a state occurs only once under the same prompt, its discounted return equals the mean for that state, making its local advantage zero. The action is still trained using the trajectory advantage.

This implementation assigns the entire trajectory reward, including the visit bonus, to the final action. Suppose the model has opened a product-detail page and both procedures ultimately buy the same product with terminal score eee.

Buy directly: buy
Visit before buying: open subpage → return to product details → buy

Buying directly receives eee immediately. Visiting first adds a bonus λ\lambdaλ, but the reward arrives two steps later, so its contribution to the current action's discounted return is multiplied by γ\gammaγ twice.

Qbuy directly=e,Qvisit before buying=γ2(e+λ). Q_{\text{buy directly}}=e, \qquad Q_{\text{visit before buying}}=\gamma^2(e+\lambda). Qbuy directly​=e,Qvisit before buying​=γ2(e+λ).

For visiting before purchase to yield a discounted return at least as high as buying directly, the visit bonus must satisfy

λ≥e(γ−2−1). \lambda\ge e(\gamma^{-2}-1). λ≥e(γ−2−1).

When both paths achieve the full score e=1e=1e=1, using γ=0.95\gamma=0.95γ=0.95 requires a visit bonus of at least approximately 0.108. Section 7.1 limits the visit bonus to below 0.0833 to preserve the priority of full-score purchases. The default value of 0.08 gives

Qvisit before buying=0.952×1.08=0.9747,Qbuy directly=1. Q_{\text{visit before buying}}=0.95^2\times1.08=0.9747, \qquad Q_{\text{buy directly}}=1. Qvisit before buying​=0.952×1.08=0.9747,Qbuy directly​=1.

The local-return difference favors direct purchase by 0.0253, but GiGPO also includes the episode-level advantage. For a two-trajectory comparison sharing this state, the episode-return difference is +0.08 in favor of visiting. The difference between the combined advantages is

ΔA=0.08+(0.9747−1)=0.0547. \Delta A=0.08+(0.9747-1)=0.0547. ΔA=0.08+(0.9747−1)=0.0547.

In a simplified example where both the prompt group and the shared-state group contain only these two paths, each once, the combined advantages assigned to visiting and direct purchase are +0.02735 and −0.02735, respectively. Discounting reduces the visit preference but does not reverse the combined signal in this example.

We train GiGPO with two random seeds and evaluate both models greedily on the same 500 tasks used for standard GRPO, with one run per task.

Model Mean terminal score Successful tasks Tasks with a designated-subpage visit before purchase
Standard GRPO 0.714 214/500 94/500
GiGPO, seed 1 0.692 202/500 2/500
GiGPO, seed 2 0.707 215/500 0/500

After both GiGPO runs, the models almost never visit the subpage, and mean terminal score does not improve. Seed 2 completes 215 tasks, close to standard GRPO's 214, but the number of tasks with a pre-purchase subpage visit falls from 94 to 0. The two-run result establishes reduced visitation. The preceding example does not explain that reduction: its combined advantage still favors visiting. Explaining the training outcome requires the actual sampled states and both advantage components.

Scoring with Group-External Historical Returns

Trajectories for the same task may take different actions but receive the same final reward. To give these actions different scores, we build a lookup table from another 7,900 training trajectories.

The table contains nine observed state–action combinations. Each entry averages the terminal returns associated with the corresponding action samples; one trajectory can contribute multiple samples. During training, a matching state and action can receive a score from this table instead of relying only on reward differences within the current prompt group. The classifications are given in Appendix B.2, under “Group-External Tables and Action-Level Verifiers.”

The table uses text matching to judge whether an option meets the request. After lowercasing the text, an option name with at least two characters is classified as a match if it appears in the user instruction, and as a non-match otherwise. For example, if the instruction contains black, selecting black is classified as a match. This rule does not use the target options in goal_options used by the environment's scorer.

On a product page, matching and non-matching actions receive scores of 0.822049 and 0.662750, respectively. These values come from mean historical terminal returns, so the table assigns a higher score to text-matching options.

When trajectories for the same prompt receive equal rewards below the maximum, we use the lookup table to adjust action advantages.

additional advantage=κ×(action score−mean score for the same state category). \text{additional advantage} =\kappa\times(\text{action score}-\text{mean score for the same state category}). additional advantage=κ×(action score−mean score for the same state category).

The mean counts each action occurrence in the current training batch that meets these conditions and has a table entry. The additional advantage is added to the original GRPO advantage and used to train the generated tokens of the corresponding action.

We compare training without the table (κ=0\kappa=0κ=0) and with it (κ=3\kappa=3κ=3), keeping all other training conditions the same. Both runs train for 75 steps.

After training, we evaluate both models on 500 held-out tasks, sampling eight trajectories per task at T=1.0T=1.0T=1.0.
